﴿And they barred (others)﴾: that is, they turned away and refused to enter Islam, or they barred others from it. Ibn Abbas (may Allah be pleased with him) said: they are the ones who fed (the polytheists) on the day of Badr. According to Muqatil, they were twelve men from among the polytheists who barred people from Islam and ordered them to disbelieve. It is also said: they are the People of the Book who disbelieved and barred those among them and others who wished to enter Islam. It is also said: it is general, applying to everyone who disbelieved and barred (others). ﴿He caused their deeds to go astray﴾: that is, He nullified and voided them. Its real meaning is that He made them lost and wasted, with no one to accept them or reward them for them, like a stray camel that is left to be lost, with no owner to protect it or look after its affairs. Or it means He made them go astray in their disbelief and sins and overpowered by them, as water goes astray in milk. Their deeds are what they did in their disbelief, which they used to call noble acts: maintaining ties of kinship, freeing captives, hospitality to guests, and protecting neighbours.

It is also said: He nullified what they did of plotting against the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and barring from the way of Allah, by granting victory over them and making His religion manifest over all religion. ﴿And those who believed﴾: Muqatil said they are some people of Quraysh. It is also said they are from the Ansar. It is also said they are believing People of the Book. It is also said it is general. He confirmed this with the parenthetical clause ﴿and it is the truth from their Lord﴾. It is also said its meaning is that the religion of Muhammad is the truth, since it cannot be subject to abrogation (naskh, the replacement of a ruling by a later one), and it abrogates other religions.

Dhalika (that) is the subject (mubtada'), and what follows it is its predicate (khabar). That is: the matter, namely the misguidance of the deeds of one of the two groups and the expiation of the bad deeds of the second group, is occurring because of the following of these ones of falsehood and those ones of truth. It is also permissible for dhalika to be the predicate of an omitted subject (mubtada' mahdhuf), meaning: the matter is as mentioned, due to this cause. In that case, the place of the prepositional phrase (al-jar wa al-majrur) is in the accusative (manstub), while on the first analysis it is in the nominative (marfu'). Al-batil (falsehood) is that which yields no benefit. And it is reported from Mujahid that al-batil is Satan. This kind of discourse is called by the scholars of rhetoric (ulama' al-bayan) "tafsir."

Kadhalika (likewise, in this manner): like that striking (al-darb), Allah sets forth for mankind their parables (yadribu Allahu lil-nasi amthalahum). The pronoun refers either to mankind, or to the two groups mentioned, with the meaning: He sets forth their parables for the sake of mankind, so that they may take heed from them.

If you ask: where is the setting forth of parables? I answer: in His making the following of falsehood a parable for the deeds of the disbelievers, and the following of truth a parable for the deeds of the believers. Or in His making misguidance a parable for the failure of the disbelievers, and the expiation of bad deeds a parable for the success of the believers.

﴿Then, when you encounter those who disbelieve, strike their necks﴾. The original is "فَضَرْبَ الرِّقابِ" (*fa-darba al-riqab*, "then striking of the necks"). Its underlying form is "فاضربوا الرقاب ضربا" (*fa-idribu al-riqab darban*, "so strike the necks with a striking"). The verb was omitted and the verbal noun was placed first, and it was then replaced by the verbal noun with its object as a genitive construction. This is a form of brevity that also carries emphasis, because you mention the verbal noun and indicate the verb through the accusative case-ending it bears. "Striking the necks" is an expression for killing. This is because what is required is striking the necks specifically, not other limbs. People used to say: "The commander struck the neck of so-and-so," "struck his nape and his crown," and "struck what his two eyes are in" (meaning, when he killed him). [[The phrase "وضرب ما فيه عيناه" may be a metaphor for his head or his face. (ع)]] This is because a person is most often killed by striking his neck, so it came to be an expression for killing, even if he is struck in some other vital part, as we mentioned in His words ﴿for what your hands have earned﴾. Moreover, this expression has a harshness and severity that the word "killing" lacks, because it depicts killing in its most grievous form, which is cutting the neck and separating from the body the member that is its top and highest part. The harshness is further increased in His words, Exalted is He: ﴿Strike above the necks and strike from them every fingertip﴾.

﴿Until you have subdued them﴾: you have increased their killing and made it severe, from "thakhin" (*thakhīn*, "thick"), which means heavy. Or: you have burdened them with killing and wounds until you have removed from them the ability to rise. ﴿Then bind them firmly﴾: take them captive.

The "wathaq" (*wathāq*, "bond"), whether with a fatha or a kasra, is the name of that with which one is bound. ﴿Then either favor [them] or [take] ransom﴾: "mannan" (*manna*, "favor") and "fida'an" (*fidā'an*, "ransom") are accusative, governed by verbs understood, meaning: "Then either you favor them, or you ransom them with a ransom." The meaning is that after taking captives there is a choice between granting them favor and releasing them, or ransoming them.

If you ask: What is the ruling on captives from among the polytheists? I reply: According to Abu Hanifa (*Abū Ḥanīfa*) and his companions, it is one of two things: either killing them or enslaving them, whichever the imam sees fit. They say concerning the favor and ransom mentioned in the verse that it was revealed on the day of Badr and then abrogated (*naskh*, "abrogation"). It is reported from Mujahid (*Mujāhid*) that: "There is no favor or ransom today; there is only Islam or the striking of the neck." It is permissible to understand "favor" to mean that they are granted a favor by leaving off killing and are enslaved. Or they are granted a favor and released in exchange for accepting the *jizya* (*jizya*, "poll tax"), and their being among the *ahl al-dhimma* (*ahl al-dhimma*, "protected non-Muslims"). As for "ransom," it means that captives from among the Muslims are ransomed with captives from among the polytheists. Al-Tahawi (*al-Ṭaḥāwī*) transmitted this as the doctrine of Abu Hanifa, but the well-known position is that he does not permit ransoming them, either with money or otherwise, for fear that they would return to fight the Muslims.

As for al-Shafi'i (*al-Shāfiʿī*), he says: The imam may choose one of four options according to what he judges to be in the interest of the Muslims. They are: killing, enslavement, ransom with Muslim captives, and favor. He argues that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) granted favor to Abu 'Urwa al-Hijabi (*Abū ʿUrwa al-Ḥijābī*). [[It is mentioned in the *Maghazi* of Ibn Ishaq and others that "he was captured on the day of Badr, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) granted him favor without ransom, then he captured him on the day of Uhud and killed him in cold blood." It was transmitted by al-Waqidi from the nephew of al-Zuhri, from his uncle, from Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib.]] And upon Thumama ibn Uthal al-Hanafi (*Thumāma ibn Uthāl al-Ḥanafī*). [[The statement "upon Thumama ibn Uthal al-Hanafi" is in the hadith of Abu Huraira in the two Shaykhs (Bukhari and Muslim), in extended form.]] And he ransomed a man with two men from among the polytheists. [[The statement "he ransomed a man with two men from among the polytheists" is a fragment of a hadith transmitted by Muslim, al-Tirmidhi and others, from the narration of 'Imran. But in it: "The Companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) captured a man from the Banu 'Uqayl, and Thaqif had captured two men from the Companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). The Prophet (ﷺ) ransomed him with the two men whom Thaqif had captured." Al-Bayhaqi, in *al-Ma'rifa*, transmitted from al-Shafi'i by this route a wording like that of the book. Then he said: "I think it is from the scribe, and the first is correct."]] All of this, according to the people of opinion (*ahl al-ra'y*), has been abrogated.

It is read "fadā" (*fadā*, with a short vowel), with fatha on the fa'. "Awzar al-harb" (*awzār al-ḥarb*, "the burdens of war") means its implements and heavy loads that cannot stand without them, such as weapons and horses. Al-A'sha (*al-A'shā*) said:

*"I prepared for war its burdens: long spears and male horses."* [[From al-A'sha. He used "awzar" (burdens) as a metaphor for the implements of war by way of explicit metaphor (*taṣrīḥiyya*). It is also possible that he likened war to beasts of burden with loads, i.e., heavy loads, by way of implicit metaphor (*makniyya*); the attribution of "awzar" is then an imaginative representation (*takhyīl*). "Rimahan" (spears) is in apposition.]]

Its burdens were so named because, since there is no escape from dragging them, it is as though they carry them and bear their weight; when the war is over, it is as though they have set them down. It has also been said that "awzaruha" means its sins, i.e., until the people of war, the polytheists, give up their polytheism and their sins by embracing Islam. If you ask: To what does "ḥattā" (*ḥattā*, "until") relate? I reply: It must relate either to striking and binding, or to favor and ransom. The meaning, on either relation according to al-Shafi'i, may God be pleased with him, is that they will continue in this state forever until there is no war with the polytheists. That is when they no longer have any power. It has also been said: until Jesus son of Mary (peace be upon him) descends.

According to Abu Hanifa, may God have mercy on him: if it relates to striking and binding, the meaning is that they are to be killed and captured until the war in general lays down its burdens, and that is when the polytheists have no power left. If it relates to favor and ransom, the meaning is that favor is granted and ransom is accepted until the war of Badr lays down its burdens, unless favor and ransom are interpreted in the manner we have mentioned.

﴿That [is so]﴾: the matter is that, or do that. ﴿Had Allah willed, He would have taken vengeance upon them﴾: He would have avenged Himself upon them through some means of destruction: by sinking into the earth, or by a quake, or by a violent wind, or by drowning, or by a devastating death. ﴿But He ordered you to fight, to test some of you by means of others﴾: that the believers should strive and be patient until they deserve the great reward, and that the disbelievers should be tested by the believers, by having them hastened by their hands to some of the punishment due to them. It is read "qutilu" (*qutilū*, "were killed") with lightening and with doubling, and "qatalū" (*qātalū*, "fought"). It is also read: ﴿So He will never waste their deeds﴾ and ﴿He will waste their deeds﴾, with the passive form, and "yudilla a'mālahum" (*yuḍillu aʿmālahum*), from "ḍalla" (*ḍalla*, "to go astray"). It is reported from Qatada (*Qatāda*) that it was revealed on the day of Uhud.

﴿He will guide them and amend their affairs and admit them to Paradise, which He has made known to them﴾: He informed them of it and made it clear to them, by means of which each person recognises his station and rank in Paradise. Mujahid said: The people of Paradise are guided to their dwellings there without error, as though they had been its inhabitants since they were created, not needing to seek directions to it. It is reported from Muqatil (*Muqātil*) that the angel appointed to guard his deeds in this world walks before him, so that everything Allah has given him becomes known to him. Or it means: He made it fragrant for them, from *al-ʿarf* (*al-ʿarf*), which is fragrance. In the words of some of them: "Its melody is like the lament of the doves, and its scent is like the fragrance of the doves" [[*ʿAzf* means singing; *al-qamārī* is plural of *qumrī*, the name of a bird; "al-ʿūd al-qamārī" is attributed to a place in the land of India, according to *al-Ṣiḥāḥ*. (ع)]]. Or it means: He defined it for them, so that each person's Paradise is bounded and separated from others, from "ʿarafa al-dār wa-āraraha" (*ʿarafa al-dār wa-ārafahā*, "he defined the house and its boundaries"); and *al-ʿarf* and *al-āraf* mean boundaries.

It is permissible to understand "favor" to mean that they are granted a favor by leaving off killing and are enslaved. Or they are granted a favor and released in exchange for accepting the *jizya* (*jizya*, "poll tax"), and their being among the *ahl al-dhimma* (*ahl al-dhimma*, "protected non-Muslims"). As for "ransom," it means that captives from among the Muslims are ransomed with captives from among the polytheists. Al-Tahawi (*al-Ṭaḥāwī*) transmitted this as the doctrine of Abu Hanifa, but the well-known position is that he does not permit ransoming them, either with money or otherwise, for fear that they would return to fight the Muslims.

As for al-Shafi'i (*al-Shāfiʿī*), he says: The imam may choose one of four options according to what he judges to be in the interest of the Muslims. They are: killing, enslavement, ransom with Muslim captives, and favor. He argues that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) granted favor to Abu 'Urwa al-Hijabi (*Abū ʿUrwa al-Ḥijābī*). [[It is mentioned in the *Maghazi* of Ibn Ishaq and others that "he was captured on the day of Badr, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) granted him favor without ransom, then he captured him on the day of Uhud and killed him in cold blood." It was transmitted by al-Waqidi from the nephew of al-Zuhri, from his uncle, from Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib.]] And upon Thumama ibn Uthal al-Hanafi (*Thumāma ibn Uthāl al-Ḥanafī*). [[The statement "upon Thumama ibn Uthal al-Hanafi" is in the hadith of Abu Huraira in the two Shaykhs (Bukhari and Muslim), in extended form.]] And he ransomed a man with two men from among the polytheists. [[The statement "he ransomed a man with two men from among the polytheists" is a fragment of a hadith transmitted by Muslim, al-Tirmidhi and others, from the narration of 'Imran. But in it: "The Companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) captured a man from the Banu 'Uqayl, and Thaqif had captured two men from the Companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). The Prophet (ﷺ) ransomed him with the two men whom Thaqif had captured." Al-Bayhaqi, in *al-Ma'rifa*, transmitted from al-Shafi'i by this route a wording like that of the book. Then he said: "I think it is from the scribe, and the first is correct."]] All of this, according to the people of opinion (*ahl al-ra'y*), has been abrogated.

It is read "fadā" (*fadā*, with a short vowel), with fatha on the fa'. "Awzar al-harb" (*awzār al-ḥarb*, "the burdens of war") means its implements and heavy loads that cannot stand without them, such as weapons and horses. Al-A'sha (*al-A'shā*) said:

*"I prepared for war its burdens: long spears and male horses."* [[From al-A'sha. He used "awzar" (burdens) as a metaphor for the implements of war by way of explicit metaphor (*taṣrīḥiyya*). It is also possible that he likened war to beasts of burden with loads, i.e., heavy loads, by way of implicit metaphor (*makniyya*); the attribution of "awzar" is then an imaginative representation (*takhyīl*). "Rimahan" (spears) is in apposition.]]

Its burdens were so named because, since there is no escape from dragging them, it is as though they carry them and bear their weight; when the war is over, it is as though they have set them down. It has also been said that "awzaruha" means its sins, i.e., until the people of war, the polytheists, give up their polytheism and their sins by embracing Islam. If you ask: To what does "ḥattā" (*ḥattā*, "until") relate? I reply: It must relate either to striking and binding, or to favor and ransom. The meaning, on either relation according to al-Shafi'i, may God be pleased with him, is that they will continue in this state forever until there is no war with the polytheists. That is when they no longer have any power. It has also been said: until Jesus son of Mary (peace be upon him) descends.

According to Abu Hanifa, may God have mercy on him: if it relates to striking and binding, the meaning is that they are to be killed and captured until the war in general lays down its burdens, and that is when the polytheists have no power left. If it relates to favor and ransom, the meaning is that favor is granted and ransom is accepted until the war of Badr lays down its burdens, unless favor and ransom are interpreted in the manner we have mentioned.

﴿That [is so]﴾: the matter is that, or do that. ﴿Had Allah willed, He would have taken vengeance upon them﴾: He would have avenged Himself upon them through some means of destruction: by sinking into the earth, or by a quake, or by a violent wind, or by drowning, or by a devastating death. ﴿But He ordered you to fight, to test some of you by means of others﴾: that the believers should strive and be patient until they deserve the great reward, and that the disbelievers should be tested by the believers, by having them hastened by their hands to some of the punishment due to them. It is read "qutilu" (*qutilū*, "were killed") with lightening and with doubling, and "qatalū" (*qātalū*, "fought"). It is also read: ﴿So He will never waste their deeds﴾ and ﴿He will waste their deeds﴾, with the passive form, and "yudilla a'mālahum" (*yuḍillu aʿmālahum*), from "ḍalla" (*ḍalla*, "to go astray"). It is reported from Qatada (*Qatāda*) that it was revealed on the day of Uhud.

﴿He will guide them and amend their affairs and admit them to Paradise, which He has made known to them﴾: He informed them of it and made it clear to them, by means of which each person recognises his station and rank in Paradise. Mujahid said: The people of Paradise are guided to their dwellings there without error, as though they had been its inhabitants since they were created, not needing to seek directions to it. It is reported from Muqatil (*Muqātil*) that the angel appointed to guard his deeds in this world walks before him, so that everything Allah has given him becomes known to him. Or it means: He made it fragrant for them, from *al-ʿarf* (*al-ʿarf*), which is fragrance. In the words of some of them: "Its melody is like the lament of the doves, and its scent is like the fragrance of the doves" [[*ʿAzf* means singing; *al-qamārī* is plural of *qumrī*, the name of a bird; "al-ʿūd al-qamārī" is attributed to a place in the land of India, according to *al-Ṣiḥāḥ*. (ع)]]. Or it means: He defined it for them, so that each person's Paradise is bounded and separated from others, from "ʿarafa al-dār wa-āraraha" (*ʿarafa al-dār wa-ārafahā*, "he defined the house and its boundaries"); and *al-ʿarf* and *al-āraf* mean boundaries.
If you support the religion of Allah and His Messenger, He will support you against your enemy, grant you victory, and make your feet firm in the places of battle or upon the highway of Islam.

﴿And those who disbelieve﴾ may be in the nominative, as the subject (mubtada', inchoative), or in the accusative, governed by a verb that the following words explain: ﴿so ruin for them﴾. It is as if he had said: "He ruined those who disbelieved."

If you ask: on what is the phrase ﴿and He misguided their deeds﴾ coordinated? I answer: it is coordinated with the verb that put ﴿ruin﴾ in the accusative, because the meaning is "He said: ruin for them," or "He decreed ruin for them."

*Ta'san lahu* is the opposite of *la'alahu*. Al-A'sha said:

*Then ruin (al-ta's) is more fitting for her than that I should say "la'a" (may you be raised up).*

*And many a wasteland, feared by the traveller, whose night-journeys are long,*
*Through which the traveller must go by night until he seeks companions to help him cross it.*

*I burdened myself with its unknown stretch, and my resolve aided me,*
*Upon it, when the mirage (al-sarab) shimmered.*

*With a camel of strength, stout and firm, when she stumbles,*
*Then ruin is more fitting for her than to say "la'a."*

Al-A'sha's meaning: many a wasteland that the traveller fears, that is, one he crosses at length. From *jabtu al-ard* (I traversed the land): I crossed it by travelling. *Al-dalja* comes from *dalaja* and *adlaja* (form *if'al* pattern); *adlaja*, in the pattern of *akrama*, means to travel by night. *Al-dalja* is a period of the night. That is, the traveller fears the exhaustion of journeying through it at night, until he seeks companions to help him on it. I burdened myself with the crossing of its unknown part, and my resolve helped me cross it at the time when the mirage shimmered, which is the shimmering seen in intense heat, looking like water, even though travel at noon is harder than travel by night. Then he said: "with a camel of strength." *Al-lawth* is also used to mean weakness, so it is one of the words with opposite meanings. *Afarnah* means coarse and stout.

It is said to the one who stumbles, "la'a laka," as a prayer for his recovery. *Ta'san lahu* is a prayer against him for his fall. He means: she does not stumble, but if she does stumble, a curse upon her is more fitting than a blessing for her. He means: stumbling and falling are closer to her than recovery and steadiness.

It is related from Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them both): he means in this world, killing, and in the Hereafter, falling into the Fire.

﴿They hated the Qur'an﴾ and what Allah revealed in it of obligations and rulings, because they had become accustomed to neglect and to giving free rein to desires and pleasures, so that this was hard on them and they found it burdensome.

Destroyed (dammara): he annihilated him; "dammara 'alayhi" means he annihilated upon him what belonged to him. The meaning is: God annihilated upon them what belonged to them of their own selves, their wealth, their children, and everything that was theirs.

﴿And for the disbelievers there are similar things﴾: the pronoun in "amthaluha" (similar things) refers either to the outcome mentioned, or to the destruction, since "tadmir" (annihilation) points to it. Or it refers to the way (sunnah) of God, based on His words, exalted is He: ﴿the way of God with those who passed away before﴾.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 47, verse 11:

*Mawla alladhina amanu* (﴿Allah is the Protector of those who believe﴾): their walī (protector) and nāṣir (helper). In the reading of Ibn Mas'ud: *wali alladhina amanu*. It is related that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was in the ravine (al-sha'b) on the day of Uhud, when wounds had spread among them, and this verse was revealed concerning that. Then the polytheists called out: "Ulu Hubal!" (Hubal is exalted!). The Muslims called out: "Allah is most high and most majestic!" Then the polytheists called out:

"A day for a day, and war is in turns (sijal). For us is al-'Uzza, and for you there is no al-'Uzza."

So the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said:

"Say: Allah is our Protector, and you have no protector. The slain are of different kinds: as for our slain, they are alive and provided for; as for your slain, they are in the Fire, being tormented."

[[Narrated by al-Tabari through the narration of Sa'id from Qatada, who said: "It has been related to us that this verse, meaning *dhalika bi-anna Allaha mawla alladhina amanu*, was revealed on the day of Uhud, while the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was in the ravine and wounds had spread among them, etc." The same. It has a witness in al-Bukhari from the hadith of al-Bara' ibn 'Azib.]]

If you say: the saying of the Exalted, *wa-ruddu ila Allahi mawlahumu al-haqq* (﴿and they are returned to Allah, their true Protector﴾), contradicts this verse. I say:

There is no contradiction between them, because Allah is the mawla of all His servants in the sense that He is their Lord and the Owner of their affairs; but in the sense of helper (nasir), He is the mawla of the believers in particular.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 47, verse 12:

They enjoy themselves (yatamatta'un): they benefit from the provision of this worldly life for a few days. And they eat (wa-ya'kulun), heedless (ghafilin), not reflecting on the outcome, as cattle eat (kama ta'kulu al-an'am) in their pastures (fi masarihiha) and their feeding places (wa-ma'alifiha), heedless of what they are about to face of slaughter and butchering. "An abode for them" (mathwa lahum): a dwelling and a station.

It is also read: "wa-ka'in," in the pattern of "ka'in" [[His words "wa-ka'in, in the pattern of ka'in": in al-Sihah, "ka'in" has the meaning of "kam" in both statement and interrogation, and there are two dialects: "ka'ayn," in the pattern of "ka'ayn" (kaʿīn), and "ka'in," in the pattern of "kāʿin." End of quote. (ʿ)]]. By "the town" he means its people, which is why He says ﴿We destroyed them﴾. It is as if He said: "How many a people, who were stronger in might than your people who expelled you, did We destroy." The meaning of "expelled you" is that they were the cause of your departure. If you ask: how does He say ﴿so there is no helper for them﴾, when this is a matter that has already passed? I say: it takes the course of the narrated present, as if He said, "We destroyed them, so they have no helpers."

Whoever has been made to see his evil deed as fair: these are the people of Makkah, for whom Satan made their polytheism and their enmity toward Allah and His Messenger appear fair.

"And whoever is upon a clear proof from his Lord," that is, upon evidence from Him and a demonstration: it is the inimitable Qur'an and the rest of the miracles, and he is the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ).

It is also read as: أمن كان على بينة من ربه. And He, exalted is He, said: ﴿سوء عمله واتبعوا﴾, which is in accordance with the wording of "man" (مَنْ), while its meaning is taken into account.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 47, verse 15:

If you ask: what is the meaning of His saying, ﴿The likeness of Paradise which the righteous have been promised: in it are rivers...﴾ ﴿...is it like one who abides in the Fire?﴾

I say: it is a statement in the form of affirmation but with the meaning of negation and denial [[Mahmud said: "It is a statement in the form of affirmation, but its meaning is negation ... etc." Ahmad said: People have mentioned many interpretations of this verse, but I have not seen anything more polished or sweeter than these subtleties that he mentioned. It only needs, to draw attention, that there is an ellipsis in the speech which must be supplied, because there is no equivalence between Paradise and those who abide in the Fire except by supposing a phrase such as "a dweller in it", by which the balance of the speech is restored and its two pans made equal. Of this same pattern is His saying: ﴿Do you consider the giving of drink to the pilgrims and the maintaining of the Sacred Mosque as equal to one who believes in Allah and the Last Day and strives in the way of Allah?﴾ For there is necessarily an ellipsis with the first or the second, so that the two parts become equal. With what you have supposed in the verse, the end of the speech agrees with its beginning, and the intended meaning becomes a comparison: after the equating of the one who holds to evil and follows his desire with the one who is at ease in Paradise, the equating of the one who enjoys Paradise and the one tormented in the Fire is denied, on the opposing attributes mentioned on both sides. This belongs to the kind of comparing a thing with itself, considered in two states, one of which is clearer in exposition than the other: the one who holds to the Sunnah is the one who enjoys the described Paradise, and the one who follows his desire is the one tormented in the described Fire. But he denied the equating between them first in terms of deeds, and he clarified that by denying the equating between them in terms of recompense second.]], because it falls under the rule of a statement introduced by the particle of denial, enters its scope, and is joined to its chain, namely His saying: ﴿Is one who has a clear proof from his Lord like one to whom the evil of his deeds has been made attractive?﴾ So it is as if it were said: "Is the likeness of Paradise like that of one who abides in the Fire?", that is, "Is the likeness of the reward of Paradise like the likeness of the reward of one who abides in the Fire?"

If you ask: why was it stripped of the particle of denial, and what is the benefit of stripping it? I say:

Stripping it of the particle of denial adds an depiction of the obstinacy of one who equates between the one who holds to clear proof and the one who follows his desire, and that he is in the position of one who affirms equality between the Paradise in which those rivers flow and the Fire in which its people are given boiling water to drink. A parallel to this is the saying of the poet:

"Do I rejoice that the noble are struck with calamity, and that I inherit a herd of she-camels thin and barren?"

[[The explanation of this witness was given earlier in volume three, page 264, so refer to it if you wish. Its corrector.]]

It is a statement denying joy at the misfortune of the noble and at inheriting the herd, stripped of the particle of denial because it falls under the rule of someone who said: "Do you rejoice at the death of your brother and at inheriting his camels?" The reason the particle of denial was dropped is the intention to depict the ugliness of the accusation directed at him [[His saying "ma azinna" means: he was accused. Related by the Sihah. (Ayn)]]. So it is as if he said to him: "Yes, someone like me rejoices at the loss of the noble and at replacing them with a herd whose yield is small [[His saying "whose yield is small", because the shasas are she-camels of little milk. And "nabl" means the large camels and the small ones too, so it is one of the words with opposite meanings. Related by the Sihah. (Ayn)]]." This is of the acceptance under which every denial lies.

"Mathal al-Jannah" means: the description of Paradise, its wondrous state; it is the subject, and its predicate is "like one who abides." His saying "in it are rivers" falls within the scope of the relative clause, as a repetition of it. Do you not see the correctness of your saying: "which has rivers in it"? It is permissible that it be the predicate of an omitted subject, "it is": "in it are rivers", as if someone said: "And what is its likeness?" and it was answered: "In it are rivers." It is also permissible that it be in the position of a circumstantial clause, meaning: "established, in it are rivers."

In the reading of Ali, may Allah be pleased with him: ﴿ amthal al-Jannah ﴾ , that is, "what are its attributes like the attributes of the Fire?" It was also read: "asin" (unchanging). It is said: the water became asin and ajin when its taste and smell changed. And he recited the verse of Yazid ibn Mu'awiyah:

"She gave me saliva not changed in its taste ... like musk mixed upon the water of grape-clusters."

[[Of Yazid ibn Mu'awiyah. "Taraddaba al-rajul rik al-mar'ah" means he sipped the woman's saliva. "Asina asan" like "ta'iba ta'aban" means its taste, smell or color changed because of its long duration. He says: she gave me her saliva, which had not changed. "Ma' al-anaqid" is a metaphor for wine, and his using it for her saliva is a clear metaphor; and she gave me musk, its state being that it was crushed upon her saliva which resembles wine, that is, as if it were so because of its fragrance. It is reported as "like musk," and that is the apparent reading; the comparison is of the kind of comparing a single thing with a compound, since he does not intend to compare the saliva with musk alone.]]

From a milk whose taste has not changed as the milks of this world change, so it does not turn sour, nor become sharp, nor have any disagreeable flavor. ﴿Delight for the drinkers﴾: "ladhdhah" is the feminine of "ladhdh," meaning delicious, or it is described by a verbal noun. It was also read with the three vowel forms: the genitive is on the attribute of wine, the nominative on the attribute of the rivers, and the accusative as a cause, meaning: for the sake of the delight of the drinkers.

The meaning: it is nothing but pure pleasure, with no loss of reason, no intoxication, no headache, and no affliction of the afflictions of wine. ﴿Clarified﴾, not having come out of the bellies of bees, so that wax and other things would mix with it. ﴿And water, boiling hot﴾: it was said that when it approaches them it scorches their faces and their scalps are stripped, and when they drink it, it cuts their intestines.

They are the hypocrites: they would attend the assembly of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and hear his speech, but they would not retain it, and they would pay it no heed except with disdain. When they went out, they would say to those among the Companions who had knowledge, "What did he just say?" (ماذا قال الساعة؟)

It was said in a mocking manner. And it was said: he was delivering a sermon, and when he criticised the hypocrites, they would leave and say that to the scholars. And it was said:

They said it to ʿAbdullah ibn Masʿud. And on the authority of Ibn ʿAbbas: "I am one of them, and I have been named among those who asked 'just now' (آنِفاً)." And it was read:

"anfan" (أنفا) on the pattern of "fa'al," in the accusative as an adverb of time [[His statement "and it was read anfan on the pattern of fa'al, in the accusative as an adverb of time": he probably means with a ḍamma. (ʿA.)]]. Al-Zajjaj said: it derives from "istaʾnaftu al-shayʾ," meaning I began the thing.

The meaning is: "What did he say at the beginning of a time close to us?"

Allah increased them in guidance by granting them success (al-tawfiq), and gave them their God-consciousness (taqwahum): He helped them to attain it. Or it means He bestowed upon them the reward for their God-consciousness.

It is related from al-Suddi: He made clear to them what they should guard against. It is also read as "wa-a'taahum" (and He gave them). And it has been said: the pronoun in "zadahum" (He increased them) refers to the saying of the Messenger (ﷺ), or to the mockery of the hypocrites.

﴿Those who are to be struck by it⦆ ... Hmm, let me render it properly below.

أَنْ تَأْتِيَهُمْ is a *badal ishtimal* (a substitute noun that is "comprehended" by the word it replaces, here an apposition of inclusion) for *al-sā'ah* (the Hour), like *an taṭa'uhum* in His saying ﴿men who are believers and women who are believers, whom you did not know, that you might trample them﴾.

It is also recited as *an ta'tihim*, with a pause on *al-sā'ah* and the conditional clause taken up anew. This is how it is written in the mushafs (copies of the Qur'an) of the people of Makkah. If you ask: "What is the response (*jazā'*) of the conditional?" I say: it is His saying ﴿then how will they have their reminder?﴾. Its meaning: "If the Hour comes upon them, how will they have their remembrance," that is, their being reminded and admonished when the Hour comes upon them. This means that reminder will not benefit them at that time, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿On that day man will remember, but how will remembrance be for him?﴾.

If you ask: "How is His saying ﴿its signs have already come﴾ connected in both readings?" I say: with the coming of the Hour, it is connected as the cause is connected to the effect, like your saying: "If Zayd honours me, then I am deserving of honour, so I honour him."

*Ashrāṭ* (the signs) means the indications. Abu al-Aswad said:

*If you have resolved to sever what is between us,*
*then the signs of its beginning have already appeared.*

[[By Abu al-Aswad. He says: if you have determined to cut off affection between us, do not conceal it, for the signs of its onset have begun to show.]]

It has been said: the sending of Muhammad, the Seal of the Prophets (ﷺ), and upon them (the prophets) from it, the splitting of the moon, and the smoke.

And from al-Kalbi: the abundance of wealth and trade, false testimony, the severing of the ties of kinship, the scarcity of the noble, and the abundance of the base.

It is also recited as *baghtatan* in the pattern of *jarbatan*, [[His saying "baghtatan in the pattern of jarbatan, and it is a strange reading": in the Qamus, *al-jarbah*, with a vowel and a doubled consonant, is a group of wild asses. In the Sihah, *al-jarbah* with a fatha is *baghtah* (suddenness), and with a doubled ba' it is a herd of donkeys. Also in it: *al-'anah* is a herd of wild asses. (Ayn)]] and this reading is strange, for its counterpart has not been found in the sources. It is related from Abu 'Amr, and how I fear that it is an error by the narrator upon Abu 'Amr, and that the correct form is:

*baghtatan*, with a fatha on the ghayn and without doubling, like the reading of al-Hasan mentioned earlier.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 47, verse 19:

When He mentioned the state of the believers and the state of the disbelievers, He said: Since you know that the matter is as mentioned, the happiness of these and the wretchedness of those, then remain steadfast in what you are upon of knowledge of the Oneness of Allah, and in humility and subduing of the self, by seeking forgiveness for your sin and the sins of those who share your religion. ﴿And Allah knows your activities, your movements, and your comings and goings in your livelihoods and your trade,﴾ and ﴿knows where you settle in your dwellings, or your movements in your life, and your abode in the graves.﴾ Or ﴿your movements in your deeds, and your abode of Paradise and Hellfire.﴾ And He is worthy that He be feared and be guarded against, and that one seek His forgiveness and mercy. And it is related from Sufyan ibn 'Uyayna that he was asked about the virtue of knowledge, and he said: Have you not heard His saying, when He began with it: ﴿So know that there is no god but Allah, and seek forgiveness for your sin﴾, so He commanded action after knowledge. Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 47, verse 20–21:

They used to claim eagerness for jihad and wish for it with their tongues, and they would say, ﴿Why has a surah not been sent down?﴾ concerning the meaning of jihad. But when a surah was sent down and they were commanded in it with what they had wished for and been eager for, they ﴿kā'ū﴾ [[Regarding his words "kā'ū": in al-Sihah (al-Jawhari's lexicon): kā'a al-kalb yak'ū, meaning: he walked on his kū' (wrist/forearm) in the sand from the intensity of the heat. (ʿ)]] and it was hard on them, and they were struck dumb, as in His saying, ﴿When fighting was prescribed for them, behold, a party of them fear men as they should fear God﴾.

﴿Muhkamah﴾: clear and explicit, not ambiguous; it admits of no meaning except the obligation of fighting. It is reported from Qatadah: every surah in which fighting is mentioned is muhkamah, and it is the most severe of the Qur'an against the hypocrites. It was called muhkamah because abrogation (naskh) does not apply to it, since fighting has abrogated what was previously forgiveness and truce, and it is not abrogated until the Day of Resurrection. It was also said: it is the newly revealed one, because at the moment of its revelation abrogation does not reach it; afterwards it may be abrogated or it may remain unabrogated.

﴿Those in whose hearts is a disease﴾: they are the ones who were on the edge, not firm of foot.

﴿Looking like one who is overcome with fainting from death﴾: that is, their eyes stare, from cowardice, dread and rage, as one looks who is seized by a swoon at death.

﴿Fa-awla lahum﴾: a threat, meaning "woe to them." It is an elative (af'al) from al-wali, which means nearness, and its meaning is an invocation against them that what is hateful should befall them.

﴿Obedience and fair speech﴾: a new (independent) sentence, meaning: obedience and fair speech are better for them. It was also said: it is a quotation of their words, meaning they said "obedience and fair speech," i.e., "our affair is obedience and fair speech." The recitation of Ubayy supports this: ﴿they say, obedience and fair speech﴾.

﴿But when the matter is resolved﴾: that is, it is made firm. Resolution and determination belong to the people of the affair, and they are ascribed to the affair only figuratively. From this is His saying: ﴿Indeed, that is of the steadfast resolves of affairs﴾.

﴿Then if they had been truthful with God﴾ in what they claimed of eagerness for jihad. Or: then if they had been sincere in their faith and their hearts had agreed with their tongues in it.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 47, verses 22–23:

*ʿAsaytum* (عسيت، عسيتم) is the dialect of the people of the Hijaz. The Banu Tamim, however, say *ʿasā an tafʿala* (عسى أن تفعل) and *ʿasā an tafʿalū* (عسى أن تفعلوا), and they do not attach the pronoun suffixes. Nafiʿ read the *sīn* with a kasra (*ʿasītum*), which is an unusual reading. The speech has been shifted from the third person to the second person by way of *iltifat* (a shift in grammatical person), so that the emphasis is stronger.

If you ask: what is the meaning of ﴿Would you, then, if you were given authority, cause corruption on the earth and sever your ties of kinship?﴾? I answer: its meaning is, "Is it expected of you that you will cause corruption?" If you ask: how can this be valid in the speech of Allah, Mighty and Exalted, who knows what has been and what will be? I answer: its meaning is that you, because of what is known of you, deserve that everyone who tests you and knows your weakness and the looseness of your bond in faith should say to you, "O people, what do you think? Is it expected of you, if you take charge of people's affairs and rule over them, given the evidences that have appeared from you and the signs that have become manifest, that you will ﴿cause corruption on the earth and sever your ties of kinship﴾, competing for kingship and being greedy for this world?"

It was also said: if you turn away from the religion and the sunnah of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), you will return to what you were upon in the Jahiliyyah of corruption on the earth, through raiding and plundering, and the severing of kinship, by fighting between relatives and burying daughters alive.

It is also recited *wa-liytum* (وليتم), and in the reading of ʿAli ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him, *tawallaytum* (توليتم), meaning: if rulers of violent tyranny take power over you, you will go out with them, march under their banner, and cause corruption along with their corruption. It is also recited *wa-tuqaṭṭiʿū* and *wa-taqaṭṭaʿū*, from *taqṭīʿ* and *taqaṭṭuʿ* (both forms of cutting off).

﴿Those are the ones whom Allah has cursed﴾ refers to those mentioned, because of their corruption and their severing of kinship. So He withheld from them His *luṭf* (divine grace) and forsook them, until they became deaf to hearing the admonition and blind to seeing the path of guidance.

It is also permissible that by ﴿those who believe﴾ He means the sincere, steadfast believers, who long eagerly for revelation when it is delayed for them. Then, when a surah concerning jihad is sent down, ﴿you see those in whose hearts is a disease﴾ among themselves complaining about it.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 47, verse 25–28:

"Al-Shaytān sawwala lahum" (Satan embellished for them): a sentence consisting of a subject and predicate, which occurs as the predicate of inna, like your saying: "Inna Zaydan 'Amrun marra bihi" (Indeed Zayd, ʿAmr passed by him). Sawwala lahum: he made it easy for them to commit grave matters; it is derived from al-sawl, which means slackness (relaxation). Whoever has no knowledge of morphology (taṣrīf) and derivation (ishtiqāq) together has derived it from al-suʾl (request/desire). [Al-Zamakhshari said: "It is derived from al-sawl, which means slackness, i.e., he made it easy for them to commit grave matters. He said: 'Whoever has no knowledge of morphology and derivation together has derived it from al-suʾl.' I say: because al-suʾl is hamzated (mahmūz), whereas sawwala is weak (muʿtall)."] "Wa-amlā lahum" (and he gave them respite): he extended them in hopes and wishes. It is also read "wa-umliya lahum," meaning: Satan misguides them and I give them respite, like His saying: "Innamā numlī lahum" (Indeed We give them respite). It is also read "wa-umliya lahum" in the passive form, meaning: they were given time, and their lifespan was extended. It is also read "suwwila lahum," and its meaning is: the scheming of Satan made it appear fair to them, with the omission of an annexed noun understood. If you ask: Who are these? I say: the Jews, who disbelieved in Muhammad (ﷺ) after the guidance had become clear to them, and his description is in the Torah. It was also said: they are the hypocrites.

"Alladhīna qālū" (those who said): the sayers are the Jews. "Wa-alladhīna karihū mā nazzala Allāh" (and those who disliked what Allah had sent down): these are the hypocrites. It was also said the reverse, and that it is the statement of the hypocrites to the Qurayẓa and the Naḍīr: "If you are expelled, we will surely go out with you." It was said that "baʿḍ al-amr" (some of the matter) refers to denying the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), or denying "There is no god but Allah," or abandoning fighting alongside him. It was also said: it is the statement of one of the two groups to the polytheists: "We will obey you in banding together against the enemy of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and in staying back from jihad with him." The meaning of "fī baʿḍ al-amr" (in some of the matter) is: in some of what you command. Or: in some of the matter that concerns you. "Wa-Allāhu yaʿlamu isrārahum" (and Allah knows their secret): it is also read "isrārahum" as a verbal noun. They said that secretly among themselves, so Allah disclosed it to them. How will they act, and what will their stratagem be then?

"Wa-quriʾa tawaffāhum" (and it is read "tawaffāhum"): it may be a past tense verb, or a present tense verb with one of its two tāʾs omitted, like His saying: "Inna alladhīna tawaffāhumu al-malāʾikah" (Indeed, those whom the angels cause to die). It is related from Ibn ʿAbbās (may Allah be pleased with them both): no one dies in disobedience to Allah except that the angels strike him on his face and his back. "Dhālika" (that) refers to the described causing to die. "Mā asakhata Allāha" (what angered Allah): concealing the description of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). "Wa-riḍwānahu" (and His pleasure): belief in the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ).

Adghanahum (their spite): their grudges. Ikhrajuha (bringing it out): exposing it to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and the believers, and showing their hypocrisy and their enmity toward them, for their hearts were seething with rage against them. ﴿La-araynakahum﴾ (Had We willed, We would have shown them to you): We would have made them known to you and pointed them out to you, so that you would recognise them by their very persons and nothing about them would be hidden from you. ﴿Bi-simahum﴾ (by their marks): by their sign, which is that Allah the Exalted would mark them with a sign by which you would know them.

It is related from Anas (may Allah be pleased with him): After this verse, nothing of the hypocrites remained hidden from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). He used to recognise them by their marks. We were once on some of the military expeditions, and in it were nine hypocrites whom the people complained about. They slept one night, and in the morning, written upon the forehead of each one of them was: "This is a hypocrite." [Al-Sha'bi related this without a chain of narration, and I have not found it.]

If you say: What is the difference between the two lams in ﴿fa-la-'araftahum﴾ and ﴿wa-la-ta'rifannahum﴾? I say: The first is the lam that enters the response to "law" (if), as in ﴿la-araynakahum﴾, repeated in the conjoined clause. As for the lam in ﴿wa-la-ta'rifannahum﴾, it occurs together with the nun in the response to an implied oath, in the manner and style of the phrase.

It is related from Ibn Abbas: "Lahn al-qawl" (the tone of speech) is their saying: "What do we gain if we obey, in terms of reward?" and they do not say: "What is upon us if we disobey, in terms of punishment?"

It was also said: Lahn means that you incline your speech toward some mode of expression, so that your companion may grasp it, such as allusion and indirect meaning (tawriya). He said:

*Indeed I have spoken to you in allusion, that you might understand, and allusion is recognised by people of discernment.*

[Lahn: turning speech away from its apparent meaning, like allusion and indirect meaning. The one who errs is called "lahin" (one who deviates), because he turns away from what is correct. That is, "so that you may understand while others do not, for the allusion is recognised by people of intellect (albab) and not by others." Albab: intellects.]

It was also said of one who errs that he is "lahin," because he turns his speech away from what is correct.

Their reports: that which is related about you and that which is told about your deeds, so that He may know their good from their bad, for the report follows the thing reported: if it is good, it is good, and if it is bad, it is bad. Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 47, verse 32:

"And He will nullify their deeds" (﴿وَسَيُحْبِطُ أَعْمالَهُمْ﴾). That is, the deeds they performed in their religion, hoping thereby for reward, because they are null and void along with their disbelief in the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). They are Qurayza and al-Nadir. Or: "He will nullify their deeds" refers to the deeds they performed and the schemes they devised in opposition to the Messenger. That is, He will render them void, so that they do not reach their aims through them; rather, they seek help through them, and they yield for them nothing but killing and expulsion from their homelands. It was also said that they are the leaders of Quraysh and those who fed (the army) on the day of Badr.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 47, verse 33:

﴿And do not render your deeds void.﴾ That is: do not nullify (yuhbitu, "cause to be void") the acts of obedience through major sins (al-kaba'ir). [[Al-Zamakhshari said: "Its meaning is: do not nullify the acts of obedience through major sins ... etc." Ahmad said: The principle of the People of the Sunna is founded on the rule that major sins other than shirk do not nullify a recorded good deed, because Allah does not wrong (anyone) the weight of an atom; and if there is a good deed, He doubles it and gives from His presence a great reward (﴿Indeed, Allah does not wrong (anyone) the weight of an atom; and if it is a good deed, He multiplies it and gives from Himself a great reward﴾). Indeed, they say that good deeds remove bad deeds, as the Generous, may He be exalted, has promised. The principle of the Mu'tazila, however, is founded on the claim that a single major sin nullifies all the good deeds preceding it, even if they were as great as the mass of the sea, because they hold with certainty that the grave sinner will abide forever in the Fire and is stripped of the mark of faith. Whoever abides forever in the Fire, his acts of obedience and his faith do not benefit him. On this basis al-Zamakhshari built his discourse and cited the reports, some of which agree outwardly with his doctrine, yet no comment is made on them as a whole without detail, because the principle mentioned above is established with certainty by evidences that necessitate it, and every qualified scholar in matters of binding and loosing is too sound to contradict it. Therefore, whatever apparently contrary report is transmitted must be returned to it by some form of interpretation. If it is an explicit text that does not admit interpretation, the proper course is to think well of the one from whom it is transmitted and to attribute the error to the transmitters. Moreover, the report cited from Ibn Umar is more apt to support the apparent meaning for the People of the Sunna, so reflect on it. As for the interpretation of the verse according to the People of Truth, it is that the prohibition concerns neglecting one of the conditions of the act or a pillar that necessitates its invalidity from its root, not that it becomes void after fulfilling the conditions of validity and acceptance.]], like His saying, ﴿Do not raise your voices above the voice of the Prophet﴾ up to His saying ﴿lest your deeds become void﴾. 

It is related from Abu al-'Aliya: The Companions of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ used to hold that no sin harms along with faith, just as no deed benefits along with shirk, until ﴿And do not render your deeds void﴾ was revealed, so they feared that major sins would nullify their deeds. [[Narrated by Muhammad ibn Nasr al-Marwazi in his book Qadr al-Salat. He said: Abu Qudama related to us, Waki' related to us, Abu Ja'far al-Razi related to us, from al-Rabi' ibn Anas with this, and he added: then ﴿And do not render your deeds void﴾ was revealed. In the book there is a marfu' hadith, narrated by Ishaq, Abu Ya'la and Abu Nu'aym in al-Hilya, from the hadith of Ibn Mas'ud. Abu Nu'aym said: Yahya ibn Yaman alone transmitted it from Sufyan, end of quote.

Yahya is weak. It is also related from Umar, narrated by al-'Uqayli, and Ibn 'Adi from the transmission of Hajjaj ibn Nusayr from Mundhir ibn Ziyad, and both are weak.]] And from Hudhayfa: [...] they feared that major sins would nullify their deeds.

And from Ibn Umar: "We used to think that none of our good deeds was unaccepted, until ﴿And do not render your deeds void﴾ was revealed. We said: What is this that nullifies our deeds? We said: The major sins, the destructive ones, and the grave transgressions. Then ﴿Indeed, Allah does not forgive that partners be associated with Him, but He forgives what is less than that for whomever He wills﴾ was revealed, so we refrained from speaking about that. We feared for those who committed major sins and hoped for those who did not commit them." [[Narrated by Ibn Mardawayh, through Abdullah ibn al-Mubarak from Bukayr ibn Ma'ruf, from Muqatil ibn Hayyan, from Nafi', from Ibn Umar with this. Muhammad ibn Nasr also narrated it by this route.]] 

And from Qatada, may Allah have mercy on him: "May Allah have mercy on a servant whose righteous deed was not nullified by his evil deed." 

It was said: Do not nullify them by disobeying the two (Allah and His Messenger). 

And from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both: Do not nullify them by showing off (riya') and seeking reputation (sum'a). And from him: by doubt and hypocrisy. 

It was said: by self-admiration ('ujb), for self-admiration consumes good deeds as fire consumes firewood. 

It was said: Do not nullify your charities by reminding of favors and by harm.
Then they died while they were disbelievers. It is said: they are the people of the well (al-qalib), and the apparent meaning is generality.

So do not falter, nor call out for peace while you are the upper ones; and Allah is with you. (Verse 35 as quoted in the commentary:) Do not be feeble, do not weaken, and do not abase yourselves before the enemy, and do not call to peace, and you are the superior ones; Allah is with you [and will not deprive you of your deeds].

Al-Zamakhshari: "And it is read as al-Salm (السلم), and both mean peace-making (al-musalama). And you are the superior ones, i.e., the more dominant, the more victorious. And Allah is with you, i.e., your helper. And it is reported from Qatada: 'Do not be the first of the two groups to bow down to the other with a request for truce.' And it is read: wa-la tadda'u (ولا تدّعوا), from idda'a al-qawm and tada'aw, when they call one another. Like your saying: 'irtamu al-sayd wa-taramawhu' (they shot at the game and shot at it one another). And tad'u (تدعوا) is jussive because it falls under the prohibition, or is in the accusative by the implied particle 'an. Like His saying, exalted is He: 'and you are the superior ones' — His saying: 'Indeka anta al-a'la' (You are indeed the Most High). And ﴿وَلَنْ يَتِرَكُمْ﴾ (and He will never deprive you) comes from watara al-rajul, when you kill for a man a slain person from his son, brother or close kin, or you bereave him; and its real meaning is: you isolate him from his relative or his property, from al-watr, which is the single one. So the loss of the worker's deed and the nullification of its reward is likened to the bereaving of the one who bereaves, and this is from eloquent speech. And from it is the saying of the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him: 'Whoever misses the afternoon prayer, it is as if he has been bereaved of his family and property' [[Agreed upon, from the hadith of Ibn Umar.]], i.e., he is isolated from them through killing and plunder."

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 47, verses 36–38:

﴿Yu'tikum ujurakum﴾ : the reward of your faith and god-fearing (taqwa). ﴿Wa-la yas'alkum﴾ : meaning, and He does not ask you for all of it (jami'uha). Rather, He limits what He asks from you to one quarter of a tenth (rub' al-'ushr). Then He said: ﴿In yas'alkumuha fa-yuhfikum﴾ : that is, if He asked you for it all, He would exhaust you (yujhidukum) and demand all of it. The ihfa' (insistent exhaustion) is intensity and reaching the utmost limit in anything. It is said: "ahfahu fi al-mas'alah" (he pressed him in the request) when he left no insistence unspent. "Ahfa sharibahu" means he uprooted his moustache.

﴿Ta-bkhalu wa-yukhrij adghanakum﴾ : that is, you would become resentful (tadghanuna) toward the Messenger of God (ﷺ). [[On the words "that is, you would become resentful toward the Messenger of God (ﷺ)": in al-Sihah, "al-dhaghn" means hatred (al-hiqd). "Tadaghana al-qawm" and "idtaghanu" mean they harbored grudges.]] Your breasts would be constricted by this, and you would show your dislike and hatred for a religion that takes your wealth. The pronoun in ﴿yukhrij﴾ refers to God, the Mighty and Majestic, meaning He would cause you to harbor resentment by demanding your wealth. Or it refers to stinginess (al-bukhl), because it is the cause of resentment.

It is also read as ﴿nukhrij﴾ with the nun, and as ﴿yukhrij﴾ with the ya' and with the ta', both with a fatha on them, and ﴿adghanukum﴾ in the nominative case.

﴿Ha'antum ha'ula'i tud'awna li-tunfiqu fi sabili Allah﴾ : ﴿Ha'ula'i﴾ is a relative (mawsul) in the sense of "alladhina" (those who), and its relative clause is ﴿tud'awna﴾ : that is, you are the ones who are called. Or, "you, O addressees, are these described people." Then He resumed describing them, as if they had said: "And what is our description?" So it was said: ﴿tud'awna li-tunfiqu fi sabili Allah﴾ (you are called to spend in the way of God). It is said that this means spending in warfare (al-ghazw). It is also said that it means zakat. As if it were said: the proof that if He demanded it all from you, you would be stingy, would hate giving, and would harbor resentment, is that you are called to pay one quarter of a tenth. Among you are people who are stingy with it.

Then He said: ﴿Wa-man yabkhal﴾ : whoever is stingy with charity and with paying the obligatory duty. ﴿Fa-la yata'addahu darar bukhlihi﴾ : the harm of his stinginess does not pass beyond him. Rather, ﴿innama yabkhalu 'an nafsihi﴾ (he is stingy only toward himself). It is said: "bakhiltu 'alayhi" and "bakhiltu 'anhu" (I was stingy toward him / from him), and likewise "danantu 'alayhi" and "danantu 'anhu." Then He informed that He does not command this nor call to it out of any need for it, for He is the Self-Sufficient (al-Ghani), to whom needs are impossible. Rather, it is for your need and poverty toward the reward.

﴿Wa-in tatawallaw﴾ : this is coordinated with ﴿wa-in tu'minu wa-tattaqu﴾ (and if you believe and fear God). ﴿Yastabdil qawman ghayrakum﴾ : He will replace you with a people other than you, who are of a different description from yours, eager for faith and god-fearing, and not turning away from them, as in His saying: ﴿wa-ya'ti bi-khalqin jadid﴾ (and bring a new creation).

It is said they are the angels. It is said they are the Ansar. From Ibn 'Abbas: Kindah and al-Nakha'. From al-Hasan: the non-Arabs ('ajam). From 'Ikrimah: Persia and Byzantium. The Messenger of God (ﷺ) was asked about these people, and Salman was beside him. He struck his thigh and said: "This one and his people. By Him in whose hand my soul is, if faith were suspended at the Pleiades, men from Persia would reach it." [[Narrated by al-Tirmidhi, Ibn Hibban and al-Hakim, and al-Tabari, Ibn Abi Hatim and others, through al-'Ala' ibn 'Abd al-Rahman from his father from Abu Hurayrah, and it has other chains from him and from others.]] And from the Messenger of God (ﷺ): "Whoever recites Surat Muhammad (ﷺ), it is a right upon God that He give him drink from the rivers of Paradise." [[Narrated by al-Tha'labi, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Wahidi, with their chains to Ubayy ibn Ka'b.]]
